*Sūtra on the Lotus of the Wonderful Law* Commentary.
Composed by Lidao Sheng.

Now, the subtle words [of the Buddha] are profound and abstruse, their wondrousness transcending the reach of hearing and sight. This has caused those who would gather and appreciate them to be few, while those who brush them aside with derision to be many.

Is this not because the Way and the secular world run contrary to one another? Since my youth, I have participated in the end of lecture sessions and have happened to take a liking to the profound mysteries; both in terms of the texts and their meanings, they are consistent.

Fubao was profoundly learned in both phenomena and principle. Since it is difficult to record forever that which is not as enduring as a mustard seed or a pebble, he briefly compiled his notes of what he heard on the day of the lecture to preserve the words of the Master, much like striking a drum to produce sound.

Furthermore, in the third month of spring in the ninth year of the Yuanjia era, at the Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu, he again revised and finalized the work, consulting various manuscripts to complete it in its entirety.

[End of] Scroll. I hope that gentlemen will attain awakening; should there be those who achieve realization, I pray you will understand that what has long been bound [in this letter] is presented as a memorial, so that the Way is not discarded because of the person.
As for the Sublime Dharma (*Saddharma*): the ultimate form is formless, and the ultimate sound is soundless. It is subtle and faint, beyond the realm of thought and trace—how could it have...?
As for those who speak of forms and words: how could it be that the reason for the divergent scriptures and differing expositions is merely this?

It is truly because the capacities and responses of sentient beings are not uniform, and thus there are myriad ways to awaken them. For this reason, the Great Sage manifested the distinctions of various branches and revealed teachings of varying degrees of disparity.
From his enlightenment at the Bodhi tree until his parinirvāṇa at Kuśinagara, he preached four kinds of Dharma wheels. The first is the wheel of goodness...

First is the Wheel of the Pure Dharma (*śuddha-dharmacakra*). This refers to the initial teaching of the one good [state] up to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), which causes one to depart from the defilements of the three miserable realms (*apāya*);

therefore, it is called "pure. Second is the Wheel of Expedient Means (*upāya-dharmacakra*). This refers to attaining the two types of *nirvāṇa* by means of the untainted factors of enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhipakṣadharma*);

this is called "expedient means. Third is the Wheel of Ultimate Reality (*tattva-dharmacakra*). This refers to destroying the falsity of the three [realms] and perfecting the excellence of the one; this is called "ultimate reality."
Indeed, there are four [turnings of the wheel], the fourth being the Wheel of the Dharma without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*). This is the discourse on ultimate convergence;
it expounds the sublime principle of eternal abiding, which is what is meant by "without remainder. This sutra takes the Mahāyāna as its central tenet.

As for the Mahāyāna, it refers to the Great Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), which begins with a single good deed and culminates in supreme wisdom. "Equality" means that the principle has no divergent paths, for all things return equally to the One Ultimate.

Furthermore, the term "Great Wisdom" (Mahāmati) is merely a designation used for its ultimate state. If one discusses the matter from beginning to end, every single atom of goodness is included therein.
As for "Vehicle" (yāna), it signifies that the principle carries all beings across, taking upon itself their suffering as its primary purpose. Regarding "Wondrous" (miao):

if one were to discuss the Tathāgata’s utterances and the presentation of his teachings, what sutra would not be wondrous? The reason this particular sutra is specifically called "wondrous" is because, whereas previously there were the three provisional [vehicles]...

To say it is not real is incorrect; to say now that the three [vehicles] do not exist is precisely what accords with principle and satisfies the truth. It is free from the falsehoods of the past and may be called "sublime.
"Dharma" refers to the essence; there is nothing that is not Dharma, for nothing surpasses the Truth. As for the "lotus flower," it is an expression of admiration for this sutra.

Indeed, among all things possessing form and appearance, none surpasses the lotus flower in its wondrousness. The beauty of the lotus lies in its first blossoming; the splendor of that initial blooming is such that—
When the essence is full within, its color, fragrance, and flavor are complete; this is called the *pundarīka*. Without the proclamation of "three," the principle is the same.
Once empty talk has vanished, the true word remains. When sincere words are disseminated, the reality of "returning to one" becomes manifest therein.
As for the "Sūtra," it is the warp and woof of the world, formed from plain silk; this warp and woof is made manifest through the practitioner.
It is the radiance of true light.

As for the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta): whenever words are established and speech is formulated, there must necessarily be a gradual progression. Since one intends to enunciate the subtle words [of the Dharma], one first manifests auspicious omens.
This, then, is the progenitor of all chapters and the sun and moon of the *Lotus Sūtra*; it likewise startles the sight and hearing of all beings.

This serves to clarify the desire to hear [the teaching]. What this sutra elucidates consists of three sections in total. From the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) through to the "Peaceful Conduct" (Anupūrva-samudācāra), these thirteen chapters clarify the three causes as being one cause.
From the "Emergence from the Earth" (Bhūmi-niṣkramaṇa) up to the "Entrusting" (Parīndanā), these eight chapters distinguish the three fruits.
From the "Medicine King" (Bhaiṣajyarāja) to the end of the "Samantabhadra" (Samantabhadra), these six chapters unify the three persons.
This is for the sake of a single person. It serves to sweep away feelings of attachment to distinct boundaries and to dissolve the stagnation of divergent streams.
Such being the case, these are the words of those who transmitted the scriptures. This is why the scriptures have been passed down through distant ages and their sublime resonance has not ceased;
it is because they possess a seal. Just as there are seals and tokens in the world, by which one cannot pass through without a gate, so too do the scriptures use five matters to serve as their seal.
"Foremost" means that it shall cause this path to be unobstructed and without difficulty. "As-it-is" (tathā) refers to speech that accords with principle;
because the words and the principle accord with one another, it is called "as-it-is. "Is" (iti) is a term signifying non-falsity; this refers to all the teachings of the Tathāgata.
I have heard it. I wish now to transmit it to those who have not yet heard it. If there were speech that was not transmitted, it would be a mere fabrication;
the matter does not lie in the ability to speak, but in the ability to transmit. This can be called the Way valuing the simultaneous forgetting [of self and other].

Abandoning myself to follow what I have heard, and hearing following from the Buddha, I clarify that this did not originate from my own mind. Therefore, the sutras and commentaries have been passed down through the ages, and their sublime track has never ceased.

"At one time. Although these words may accord with reason, if they do not coincide with the opportune moment, they are likewise a hollow proclamation. Therefore, "at one time" is explained next. As for "time":

when the capacities of sentient beings move the Sages, the Sages are able to manifest their response; when the paths of the mundane and the sacred intersect, the excellent opportunity is not lost—this is called "one time."
The Buddha was in Rājagṛha. Although the Dharma-body is omnipresent, if the location where it was taught were not recorded, it would still be like a turbulent wave;
thus, one cannot help but provide a prologue to certify the teaching. This mountain has five locations; at which of these was it spoken?
It was at the Gṛdhrakūṭa Parvata Vihāra.
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—if one hears this alone, it is likewise difficult to believe.
Even if we and ordinary people have not yet attained solitude, those who hear it together with us are all our superiors; citing them serves as proof for the sutra.

"Bhikṣu" is a general term for one who has destroyed evil. The reason why the śrāvakas are mentioned first and the bodhisattvas later is that this represents the sequence of inner and outer [realization].
This is different. Internally it has limitations, yet externally it is without fixed direction; thus it is appropriate that it be so. It also symbolizes the Buddha’s transformation of beings:
from the near to the distant, the Way is omnipresent. As for its greatness, among the ninety-six types of heterodox paths, it stands as their preeminent leader.
Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya: *Ājñāta* means "one who has attained" (in the Song translation, it is rendered as "having attained the wisdom of no-more-learning");
*Kauṇḍinya* is his clan name. Because he was the first to attain the Way, he was named accordingly. Mahākāśyapa: *Mahā* means "great"; *Kāśyapa* is his clan name.
Since he was already advanced in years and furthermore possessed great virtue, he was called thus. Kāśyapa is a Brahmin clan name. Uruvilvā... [text ends]
"Śrāvastī" refers to the grove of Uruvilvā Kalandaka; because he constantly resided in this grove, it was named after that location.
"Gayākāśyapa": Gayā is the name of a city; because he lived on the outskirts of this city, he was named after it. "Nadī": this is the name of a river;
because he was born on the banks of this river, it became his surname. "Śāriputra": this is the name of his mother; her eyes resembled [a śāri bird]..."
Śāriputra: This is because of his name. "Pu" means son. Śāri-mātṛ was a woman of high talent and skill in debate, renowned throughout the world;
therefore, he was named Śāriputra after his mother's name. Mahāmaudgalyāyana: His courtesy name was Kolita, and he was born into the Brahmin caste.
Mahākātyāyana: He was of the Brahmin clan of South India, and thus [was named] after his original...
"Family name" refers to the designation *Anuruddha*, which in the Song language means "Unvanquished. *Kapphiṇa* is his personal name; it has no equivalent translation [into Chinese].
*Gavāmpati*: *Gava* means "ox," and *pati* means "foot. Because he was born with feet resembling those of an ox, he was thus named "Ox-foot.
*Revata* is the name of a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). He was born when this mansion was appearing, and so it was made his name.
Piliṅgavatsa: *Piliṅga* is his given name; *Vatsa* is his clan name. Bakula: this means "well-nourished" or "robust.
Mahākauṣṭhila: this means "Great-Knee. Nanda: this means "Joy"; he was the younger brother of the Buddha. Sundarananda:
this means "Gentle," "Upright," or "Joyful. Pūrṇa is his clan name. Maitreya... [text ends]
Maudgalyāyana is also called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. "Maitrāyaṇī" is the name of his mother; she possessed great eloquence and wisdom and was well-known to many people.
Because her mother was noble, he was referred to by her clan name. He was named after his mother, hence the appellation "Son of Maitrāyaṇī."
Subhūti is named Shanji (Good Fortune); he is also called Kongsheng (Born of Emptiness). Ānanda was of such upright and handsome appearance that all who saw him were filled with joy;
because he was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, he is called Huānxī (Joyful).

Rāhula—translated in the Song dynasty as Bùfàng (Not Released)—was held in the womb for six years, hence he is called Bùfàng. These śrāvakas were well-known to all; their virtues were manifest within, and their names resounded abroad.

As for those outside [the monastic community], from afar and near, all have turned their hearts toward them—who does not know them? Thus, in listing names and extolling virtues, it is clearly shown that the Dharma of the Hīnayāna is itself the path of the Bodhisattva.
Next, the assembly of nuns is listed, beginning with Mahāprajāpatī. "Mahāprajāpatī" means "Great Path of Compassion" (Dà Àidào) in the Song language.
Then there is Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula; "Yaśodharā" means "Holding Fame" (Chíyù) in the Song language.

Shengyuan heard that there were eighty thousand bodhisattvas. As for the śrāvakas, their primary purpose is the exhaustion of suffering; therefore, it was said first that they had "cast off their burdens.

The path of the bodhisattvas, however, involves a resolve that extends universally; they do not focus on the removal of their own fetters, but solely desire to rescue all beings according to the proper method.

It is solely through the dhāraṇīs, up to the four types of eloquence; therefore, it first sets forth the wondrous arts of his majestic conduct, concluding with the statement that he has delivered immeasurable people.
"Making offerings to all Buddhas" refers to the practices performed in past lives. "Cultivating the body with compassion" follows below, clarifying the merit of the Bodhisattva’s three karmas.
"Compassionately nurturing the weak and the lost" refers to cultivating the body with compassion; as for the mention of the "body," [it refers to...]
This encompasses both speech and mind. "Thoroughly penetrating great wisdom" refers to what he has attained within himself; in the context below, it simply means "penetration.
"Reaching the other shore" merely describes the ultimate limit of his attainment. His fame is heard everywhere, while his virtue is manifest within.
His fame spread abroad. Once his achievements and reputation were established, they became widely known outside [the realm].

Śakra-devānām-indra is the second Lord of the Devas; he commands the four Guardian Kings of Heaven and issues decrees to control the various dragons and spirits, ensuring they do not recklessly harm sentient beings.
Furthermore, he constantly cultivates merit, which causes the sun and moon to be brilliant and pure. He frequently acts as their counterpart in manifesting their splendor.

He is the lord of these [spirits]; therefore, he is mentioned at the beginning. As for the eight classes of spirits and deities, "deities" (shen) are those capable of assuming various forms and changing their appearances, appearing either as celestial beings or as humans;
thus, they are placed in the interval between these two categories. As for the Four Great Heavenly Kings, they reside on the eastern side of Mount Sumeru.
The one in the east is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the one in the south is named Virūḍhaka; the one in the west is named Virūpākṣa; and the one in the north is named Vaiśravaṇa.
These are the eight Dragon Kings (Nāgarāja) under the command of Śakra Devendra. All these Dragon Kings are named Avalokita-pramodita; they manifest in human form and reside in the city of Rājagṛha.
If there is a severe drought, the king and his ministers all go to seek them, whereupon they cause sweet rain to fall, moistening the earth.
There is one country where people see [them] and rejoice; therefore, it is named "Joyful" (Kāmadhātu).

There are four Kinnara Kings—translated in the Song dynasty as "human-non-humans"—whose forms are upright and handsome, and who have a horn upon their heads; they are the deities of the Heavenly Emperor who hold musical instruments.
There are four Gandharva Kings, who are likewise deities of celestial music; they differ only in that they lack horns. As for the Asura Kings—"Asu" means... [text fragment].
There is none. Asura means "wine. In the past, he was of the Brahmin caste; as one of pure conduct who did not drink wine, he was given this name.
Garuḍa—translated in the Song language as "Sky-Walker"—is the deity of the golden-winged bird. Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī: Vaidehī is the mother's name.
Ajātaśatru—translated in the Song language as "Unborn Enemy"—was so called because while she was pregnant with him...
He always harbored an evil mind toward King Bimbisāra; therefore, he was named Ajātaśatru. Because he was born of Vaidehī, he is called the son of Vaidehī.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly. Since his virtue was profound and his majesty surpassed the sun and moon, he caused gods and humans [to gather].

They gather together; with hearts united in their shared veneration, all living beings are blessed. This ensures that one departs empty-handed but returns with substance. As for "making offerings and showing reverence":
making offerings consists of relinquishing wealth, while reverence consists of solemnizing one's deportment. As for "honoring and praising":

"honoring" refers to the sentiment of exalting and cherishing [the recipient], a feeling that exceeds that held toward a sovereign or a father. "Praising" means that, having rejoiced in the virtues within, one expresses them through outward hymns of praise. Thus it is said.

The Mahāyāna sūtras accord with the external [teachings] of the Three Vehicles; yet their traces contradict their underlying principle. If one clings to the literal text while deviating from the essential intent, how could one not be startled by the proclamation of the One Vehicle?
When about to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he first guided and reached their minds by preaching the *Anantamukha-sūtra*.

Since they had long been stalled by the traces [of the Three Vehicles], hearing suddenly that there were no three vehicles caused them to abruptly abandon their former preferences. If those former preferences are abandoned, then—like gazing toward the shore—[they will be unable to cross].
To turn back and look toward the shore to return is where the Great Way is abandoned; therefore, one must proceed by gradual stages.

"Immeasurable Meaning" (*ananta-artha*) refers to the fact that all such characteristics are non-existent, such that there is neither more nor less, neither deep nor shallow. It speaks solely of the practice for attaining Buddhahood.

When the words and their purport are substantial, it is called "Meaning"; when the principle is vast and liberates one from the suffering of the long journey, it is the Mahāyāna. It is solely Bodhi...

The Bodhisattva is able to learn; it is for his sake that this is expounded. This is the teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas. Since Bodhisattvas have not yet exhausted the ultimate principle, they should be instructed by means of this teaching.

It is what the Buddha protects and keeps in mind; the Buddha has fully exhausted the principle and completely guards it so that it is never forgotten or lost. It is for the sake of the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings. Now, movement and stillness belong only to things; how could the Sage be like them?

To exhaust the principle and perfect one's nature is called the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings. From [this... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist scripture, likely related to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* or a similar Mahāyāna text. The translation reflects the technical terminology and philosophical context of such literature.)
When this samādhi arises, whatever is spoken cannot possibly be erroneous; therefore, it must be clearly understood. Once one has entered this samādhi, the spirit moves Heaven and Earth:
Heaven rains down *mandārava* flowers, and the earth trembles. Since Heaven and Earth have been thus moved, [the response follows].

How could people remain silent? Since auspicious omens have manifested as portents, there must be extraordinary teachings [to follow]. The sentiments of the age are inclined toward them, and their doubts are likewise profound.
As these deep doubts accumulate, awakening will also be profound. The falling of the four flowers from heaven signifies that the four fruits are not substantial;
the shaking of the earth signifies that the four fruits are not fixed. It also reveals the great awakening and its distribution throughout the six realms of existence. Furthermore—
This clarifies impermanence. Contemplate the Buddha with a single mind; know that there must be a different teaching. Wait to hear the marvelous proclamation.
The light from the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows manifests the Middle Way of the One Vehicle, free from the defilements and obscurations of the Two Vehicles.
It is revealed upon the forehead to demonstrate the mark of impartial merit. Once this light shines forth, this wisdom will surely be bestowed. It illuminates the East, for the East is the assembly.

Compared to the past, this demonstrates that the One Vehicle is the subtle essence of the Three Vehicles; it also clarifies that those who have attained great awakening do not exhaustively illuminate because they remain in profound stillness (*míng*).
Although the eighteen thousand [rays] previously illuminated only one direction, if one wishes to clarify this light, there is nothing it cannot illuminate.

Therefore, these eighteen thousand are employed to symbolize that illumination is omnipresent within the One. As for "penetratingly illuminating above and below," this clarifies that the Way is without...

He was not there. Yet he saw that land in its entirety. The reason he and the other were able to see one another was to demonstrate that the True Path is empty and pervasive, without obstruction or impediment.
As for why the sentient beings of the six realms of existence see the six paths, it clarifies that these exist because of delusion.
Furthermore, seeing the various Buddhas—having already seen the delusions of the six realms—one must necessarily have those who turn back from such delusion. To turn back...

As for those who are deluded, none other than the Buddha [can guide them]. Upon hearing the sutras and Dharma taught by the various Buddhas, one who wishes to reverse their delusion and attain liberation must hear the Dharma;
this next statement refers to "hearing the exposition of the sutras. All those who practice and attain the Way are disciples who have reversed their delusions.

Through various causes and conditions, it is clarified that the spiritual faculties of sentient beings are not uniform, and they attain awakening in myriad different ways—some through giving, and so forth.

Regarding the precepts, they may be based on supernatural transformations; hence the term "various. Furthermore, as for seeing the various Buddhas entering nirvana, this is shown to them by way of analogy.
One should know that Śākyamuni’s parinirvāṇa is not far off; this is intended to direct the minds of beings toward the distant [goal] and to strengthen their earnest quest for the Dharma.

Maitreya thought to himself: "This auspicious omen has appeared because [the time] has arrived. For a long time, the multitude’s minds have been mired in stagnation and their attachments have been deeply rooted.
Suddenly beholding these wondrous signs from before, they are filled with bewildered doubt. Since Maitreya occupies the station of the Regent, he shares this intention;
it rises within the hearts of the age, and as he seizes upon this opportunity to doubt, his doubt has accumulated so deeply that his awakening will likewise be swift. Thus thought Maitreya.

As for the one who acts as the principal interlocutor, it is because those who seek a definitive resolution must necessarily obtain clarity and correctness. Now, regarding Mañjuśrī’s inquiry up to the emission of light:
the reason he first entered samādhi, caused flowers to rain down, and shook the earth was to manifest the One Vehicle (Ekayāna);
thus, the light of the One Vehicle is indicated here at the end. Furthermore, the One Vehicle is the fundamental intent of this assembly; therefore—
Maitreya now first asks about the emission of light; these [questions] are raised alternately, both preceding and following one another, each having its own underlying meaning.

Next, he should ask about the raining of flowers and the shaking of the earth, which are omitted here but shall be fully addressed within the verses. He asks in verse: (The composition of these verses...)
There are four general reasons: first, for the sake of future followers; second, for the sake of those who have not yet attained realization;
third, because the prose version was brief, these verses expand upon it; and fourth, to express boundless emotion through song, dance, and performance.

Although Maitreya has previously roughly inquired into its essentials, he now speaks of the matter in full detail. As for why the name of Mañjuśrī is first indicated, it is so that the people of the time...

My feelings are focused upon his ears and eyes; my admiration has reached its peak. Later, when I heard his words, my sentiments remained without any interval of doubt. Now I shall briefly explain this.

Since what I have seen and heard is so vast, it is difficult to exhaustively describe it all in words. As for what I saw in that land, from the beginning, there were many verses concerning various causes and conditions and various forms of faith and understanding.
"Various" means that these matters—whether regarding precepts or giving—are not of a single kind. From the beginning...
The listing of the practices of the six perfections lacks a fixed sequence; it may be understood through reflection.

The reason for causing those present at this assembly to see that good and evil is to lead them to abandon evil and cultivate goodness, and also to demonstrate that the light of wisdom reflects everything without exception.
Mañjuśrī said to Maitreya: "As I contemplate it, the profound and deep mystery of ultimate principle transcends the realm of numerical calculation."
This is the preface. Were it not for one who has personally realized the profound principle to its ultimate depth, by what means could this [teaching] be so clearly articulated?

One must surely entrust the "sculptor of Ying" to Mañjuśrī; yet even those who still harbor doubts must realize that clarity lies only with the Buddha. This is because of a sincere desire to cultivate firm faith.

From here below, there are four sections, which serve as proof that the *Lotus Sūtra* was to be preached. Regarding the first section: Mañjuśrī, knowing that the principle is already subtle and profound, did not dare [to speak of it himself].
He pointedly rebuked [the assembly] and spoke with detailed clarity, saying: "I now reflect that I wish to preach the Great Dharma.
Good sons, in the past, under various Buddhas, I have witnessed this very same omen. This second section cites the past to corroborate the present.

Although the past and present differ, their Way is not distinct. Since the omen of the past was such as this, and the Great Dharma was preached, one should know that it is likewise so for the present Śākyamuni.
It is clear that the auspicious signs of Kāśyapa must signify the preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Previously, it was stated simply that this had already occurred in the past;
now, authentic evidence will be cited, namely the case of Candrasūryapradīpa. The Tathāgata speaks according to the meaning, and thus his names are infinite.

Why is it that we now speak only of the ten directions? "Ten" represents the ultimate limit of number; it symbolizes that the principle of the Tathāgata is perfectly complete and without deficiency, and that the Way is omnipresent.
Therefore, the number ten is employed as a metaphor. As for the term "Tathāgata": although the myriad dharmas differ, they are all identical within the single Suchness (tathatā).

The Sage’s essence comes forth to transform sentient beings; thus, he is called the Tathāgata. He is the Worthy One of Offerings and the Ultimate Path, a fertile field capable of producing the wondrous.

As for the fruit [of his practice], both the marks [of his body] and [his attachment to] them have been forgotten; this may be called making offerings to the *Samyaksaṃbuddha*. His wisdom is all-pervasive, hence it is called "universal" (*vibhu*);

this knowledge is free from error, hence it is called "right" (*samyak*). Regarding the "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (*Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*): his actions of body, speech, and mind proceed in accordance with wisdom, which is termed "knowledge and conduct.

Since his wisdom is already universally knowing, his conduct is likewise fully perfected. As for the "Well-Gone One" (*Sugata*), whether in life or after death, he acts for the sake of beings, and there is nothing that does not bring them benefit.
His traces ended beneath the twin trees; he passed away for the sake of sentient beings, and because of this, beings were further benefited—how could this not be virtuous?
One who understands the world takes the five aggregates to be the world; the Tathāgata has thoroughly realized the world and further understood its fetters and bonds.

He is the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*), whose human excellence and Way are absolute, with none equal to him. He is the Tamer of Men (*puruṣa-damya-sārathi*); regarding the various evils of body and speech that are stubborn and difficult to tame, the Buddha...

He is able to subdue them and further disciplines sentient beings; thus he may be called a "Great Man" (puruṣa). As a Teacher of Gods and Humans, having perfected the sublime art of training and disciplining, he is fit to be the Teacher of Gods and Humans.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*): "Buddha" means awakening; he awakens to birth and death and is endowed with the ten aforementioned virtues, and is therefore collectively termed the World-Honored One.
"Good in the beginning" refers to the *śrāvakas*; "good in the middle" refers to the *pratyekabuddhas*; "good in the end" refers to...
Regarding the Bodhisattvas: next, the persons of the three vehicles are listed to set forth their respective matters. In the past, these three types of transformation were also taught;

their meaning is the same as it is now. Thus, twenty thousand Buddhas are cited. The reason for citing twenty thousand Buddhas to testify to Śākyamuni is that they secretly represent the transformation of the two vehicles in order to manifest the excellence of the One Vehicle.
Therefore, it is necessary to extensively cite many Buddhas; the more numerous these individuals are, the greater the significance.
The Way is fundamentally one. It has eight sons. The reason for the emergence of these eight sons from the side is twofold:
first, to demonstrate that Mañjuśrī’s mind encompasses all time, such that he was the teacher of Dīpaṃkara, and Dīpaṃkara, in turn, was the teacher of Śākyamuni.
Since this is so, how could the words spoken by Mañjuśrī be erroneous? Second, it serves as an introductory perspective for opening the gradual path to Long Life.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached the Mahāyāna sūtra; this second section cites the present to prove that the auspicious signs of the current time are identical [to those].
Subhāṣita had eight hundred disciples. The reason he produced eight hundred disciples was because he wished—
This clarifies that Maitreya is not only contemporary; he previously consulted Mañjuśrī and received his teachings as a disciple.
That he now again poses questions demonstrates his certainty regarding the future. At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from samādhi.

This is the fourth section, which speaks of the time in that direction. Since this intends to speak of sixty kalpas, how could it be taken literally? It serves to manifest the profound respect for the Dharma.

Because his mind was directed toward it, he expressed it thus by way of time. He entered nirvana at midnight. Because his earnest desire to seek the Dharma was so profound, the reason he later recorded that Dezang would become a Buddha was to lead those like himself who were on the precipice.
When they suddenly heard that the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, they thought there would be no more sages thereafter and consequently ceased their efforts on the path of practice.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] recorded that Dezang would become a Buddha because worldly people seek fame and profit.
People generally delight in preserving what is near while neglecting what is distant; therefore, I now deprecate this [habit]. To admonish people to cut away this mind, I shall speak in verse.
Regarding the method of versification, sometimes the preceding prose is omitted and not versified, and sometimes the preceding prose does not exist while the verse does;

thus, it is difficult to establish a fixed standard. One may adapt the rules according to the circumstances as required. As for the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is no falsity of the two vehicles; it speaks only of the Great [Vehicle].
The true reality of the vehicle.

In the second chapter, "Expedient Means," [the Buddha] formerly concealed his traces within the three vehicles, and the multitude took him to be such; now he wishes to reveal the single reality and demonstrate the true and correct [path]. By means of...
It is not that this is not clear; therefore, the chapter is titled "Expedient Means" (*upāya*). Since the former three vehicles are designated as expedient means, the One Vehicle is revealed;
thus, although it is not explicitly stated here, it is self-evident. If one were to call it the "Chapter on the One Vehicle," the principle might seem to be reducible to a single unity;
hence, by saying "expedient means," the ultimate state beyond all praise is indicated.
He rose serenely from samādhi. Now, since the profound essence is entrusted to it, the subtle words are likewise deep.
That the flowers rained down and the earth shook above, that Maitreya harbored doubts and Mañjuśrī resolved them—was this not to stir those lost in delusion and to cleanse their minds?
Once the mind is vast and open, one is capable of receiving the One Vehicle; furthermore, the Sage established these rules to accord with the responses of sentient beings.

Arising from meditative concentration, he spoke; his words were invariably in accord with ultimate reality. Because they were in accord with reality, the hearts of those who received them naturally became profound and sincere.
He addressed Śāriputra. The reason for addressing him was that his outward traces lay within the vehicle of the śrāvaka, making him a proximate vessel;

yet his actual illumination surpassed that of others, making him fit to receive this exalted teaching. His wisdom is exceedingly deep; though his words may differ in myriad ways, their underlying intent is to manifest the truth.

First: The object contradicts the meaning of the words. This results in a profoundity within wisdom; it is not that the object is profound because of this wisdom being profound, but rather that the object is profound relative to wisdom.
This is merely an expression lamenting one's own failure to reach it; how could it be a praise of wisdom? As for the gateway of wisdom: since wisdom resides in speech, speech constitutes the gateway.

It is not only that wisdom is incomprehensible, but the gateway is likewise difficult to understand. To understand the gateway is to penetrate the three negations (trividha-niḥsvabhāva). Negation—[end of fragment].
How is it difficult to understand? It is that which cannot be known by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. If this is so, then all three vehicles are provisional;
yet the Mahāyāna does not contradict the reason why it is "Great," and therefore it is not mentioned [in the same context]. The two vehicles, however, run contrary to the fundamental principle.
It is said that [the Buddha] did not know. Why is this? Regarding such an unprecedented phenomenon (*adbhuta-dharma*), if one does not understand the reason for it, how could one believe in it?

It must be explained further. That the attainment of the ultimate through such accumulated practice is unprecedented—that which might otherwise be considered beyond measure—is now expressed through the "phrase of wisdom" (*jñāna-pada*).
This explains the result by means of the cause; it is taught according to what is appropriate, such that its traces accord with external reality. From...

The traces must obscure the essential meaning; when the essential meaning is obscured, it is difficult to understand. This concludes the section on the "Gates of Wisdom. Having already explained the reasons for this, the subtle meaning shifts slightly.

From my attainment of Buddhahood until now, up to the point where I have caused others to be free from all attachments, I have generally praised the Buddha’s wisdom; this explanation follows accordingly.

This was spoken by Śākyamuni. This phrase was composed as a chapter title. Since the preceding passage spoke of "according to what is appropriate" (*yathā-yogam*), there may be those who give rise to attachment;

therefore, it is necessary to clarify this further. To speak of "according to what is appropriate" means to act in accordance with what is suitable for the illness. Illnesses have ten thousand manifestations, and the teaching must necessarily be without fixed form.

All of these are fundamentally intended to guide beings toward detachment from clinging; were it otherwise for even a single day, there would be no principle by which attachment could be relinquished.

Thus it is said that since his attainment of Buddhahood, [the Buddha’s] internal mastery of skillful means (*upāya*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) has been perfected, while externally, his every word is nothing but a skillful means of deliverance.
Furthermore, to clarify why he has perfected these skillful means: it is because his excellent conditions of illumination are perfect and without obstruction.

This is because it has reached the ultimate. That the merit of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) penetrates deeply into the boundless explains why the perfection of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana-pāramitā*) is fully perfected.
Although various distinctions are skillfully used to explain all phenomena, since it is said that there is no fixed direction, the phrasing may appear to diverge from reason;
one must therefore further clarify the differences between the three vehicles. These are called "various" (*vividha*), while using the three to represent the one is called...

Skillful exposition: ten thousand words converge upon the same truth, possessing no further divergent flavors; they accord with others without opposition—this is called "gladdening the hearts of the multitude.
The preceding clarified internal realization; this clarifies external transformation. Cease, Śāriputra, there is no need for further discourse.

Having already clarified that the three vehicles are not real, one should next clarify that this is the One Vehicle. Although it is said they are not real, they still have not yet reached the point of being truly appropriate. Not yet...
It would be truly startling to those who cling to their own views; if one were to speak further, they would surely be struck with alarm and doubt.

Therefore, he called out to stop, for how could it be said that by not speaking he merely intended to dispel their doubts? Although he did not explicitly state "one" earlier, he had already roughly indicated the meaning;
thus he said there was no need to speak further. True reality (*bhūtatathatā*) has no falsehood of the two vehicles, but is solely the truth of the One Vehicle. Such is its characteristic.

Nature (*svabhāva*). These eleven matters refer to the conditions for all virtues. Just as smoke is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of fire and its capacity to burn is its nature, so too do characteristics pertain to the external while nature presides over the internal.

"Body" (*tattva*), "nature," and "characteristic" are general designations for these. Regarding "power" (*bala*) and "activity" (*kriyā*): that which possesses capability but has not yet been employed is called power;

that which performs a function through actual application is called activity. Regarding "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): that which is capable of producing is the cause; that which supports and sustains is the condition. Regarding "fruit" (*phala*).

"Retribution" (*pāka*) refers to the fulfillment of one's aspirations; this is called "fruit" (*phala*). That which is concentrated through the sequence of kalpas is called "retribution. Regarding "beginning and end":

the commencement of myriad virtues is the "end," while the culmination of the Buddha’s wisdom is the "beginning. Only the Buddha thoroughly understands these various meanings and comprehends their ultimate source.
Therefore, he concludes by saying, "Ultimately equal," excluding those among the assembly of bodhisattvas whose power of faith is not yet firm. Previously, the Buddha spoke of three [vehicles].

Now, it is said that there is none; yet, not even one has been mentioned. This intention is difficult to fathom, and those who can fathom it are few. Therefore, various individuals are listed extensively.

Those who are "firm and stable" are those from the eighth stage (bhūmi) upward; they alone are able to fathom that the Buddha will preach the One Vehicle (ekayāna), which is why they are excluded [from the list of those who do not understand].

The followers of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) naturally cannot fathom it, as can the bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, those of intellectual understanding, and the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.

From the first stage to the seventh stage, how could it be said that [the Bodhisattvas] do not know? It is merely stated thus because one wishes to exalt and beautify the One Vehicle so that people may revere and believe in it.
The words are no different; the principle is only the single ultimate. Since the words accord with the principle, it is said that "the words are no different."
At that time, among the great assembly, there were as many as twelve hundred people whom the Buddha had previously silenced and not spoken to, for he wished to cause them to harbor doubt.

Now, they are even more bewildered by their uncertainty. These śrāvakas, having heard the Buddha extensively praise this path as being profoundly deep, do not know where its essential meaning lies—the single principle of liberation. [They think: "We too have attained this Dharma; the merit of the Three Vehicles..."
Virtue, though said to differ in degree of excellence, is no different when it reaches the place of eternal rest in *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, it is said that since liberation is one and the same, I do not know to what purpose the meaning of the most earnest praise previously offered was directed.
Śāriputra knew that the minds of the fourfold assembly were filled with doubt; he perceived the prevailing sentiment of the times and seized the opportunity to inquire.

As their doubts accumulated, their desire for a definitive resolution reached its peak. Yet, regarding the Dharma attained at the site of enlightenment—its path being lofty and its principles profound—who could possibly pose such questions?

If the Buddha had not spoken, it would have appeared as though he were longing for the Dharma; therefore, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and, without being asked, spoke of his own accord to praise the profound and immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas—this is what this verse describes. The Buddha told Śāriputra, "Stop, stop;
there is no need to speak further. The Buddha’s initial "stop" was intended to halt Śāriputra's doubts, but Śāriputra said, "Speak, and then I shall stop."
Because of these doubts, he requests again. Although the two statements differ in wording, their purpose in dispelling doubt is the same.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: "Since you have already made this earnest request three times—now, when a sage establishes his teaching, the words must necessarily proceed gradually, and awakening likewise occurs in stages.
Since you have now made this third request, your manifold doubts shall be dissolved. When your manifold doubts are dissolved, then..."

My heart rejoices at hearing this without interruption. As for the reason for my three requests, it was not that I, a sage, desired it so; rather, it was because the spiritual capacity [of the audience] required it.

From here on, there are five sections clarifying the meaning: first, distinguishing between the true and the false; second, correctly elucidating the path of the ultimate unity of the fundamental principle;
third, clarifying that the tracks of all Buddhas of the three periods are mysteriously identical; and fourth, explaining the reason why [the teaching] was spoken.

Regarding the "Three Vehicles," it was not the intention of the Sage to be so; he did so out of necessity. As for the "five thousand people who withdrew"—those who had attained or failed to attain the five branches of knowledge—this first section distinguishes between the genuine and the spurious.
It speaks truly that when the presentation is about to begin, the genuine and the spurious will naturally be discerned.

This is like the sun and moon having already shone, whereby the white and the black are clearly distinguished. The reason for manifesting these traces is merely to admonish and rectify the sentiments of the times.
If those of overweening pride do not participate in this auspicious assembly, let them take joy in the arrival of this occasion and spur themselves toward faith and awakening.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, continuing until the passage "no longer having branches or leaves. This second section clarifies the path of ultimate unity:
once the profuse twigs have perished, the sturdy trunk remains. Though what is taught follows what is appropriate and is spoken in accordance with the capacities of beings, even so—
Although three [vehicles] are taught, the underlying intention remains fixed upon the manifestation of the One; thus it is said that the intended meaning is difficult to comprehend.

It is solely for the sake of the great cause and condition (*mahāntam artham hetum*) that [the Buddha] appears in the world. Having already provided a rough indication of the fundamental principle above, this now explains it further.

Since it was stated that the three vehicles are expedient means, it is now clarified that there is but the One. The Buddha is the ultimate One; he appears in the world to manifest this Oneness. This is the principle.
Even if there were three [aspects], the Sage could still manifest as three; however, in principle, there are not three, but only the wondrous One.
Therefore, it is said that he appears in the world for one great matter: to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The profound purport of these subtle words is revealed herein. These four phrases, from beginning to end, constitute a single meaning. This is truly because of sentient beings.

The Buddha’s wisdom and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) are inherently present; they merely do not manifest because of defilements and obstructions. When the Buddha removes these, they are brought to fulfillment. One interpretation states:

from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, the gradual elimination of afflictions (*kleśa*) is called "opening" (*kai*); the unimpeded radiance [that follows] is called "purity" (*viśuddha*).
To demonstrate the Buddha’s wisdom and vision to sentient beings, it was previously stated that their inherent portion exists; through the present teaching, it is now realized.
If accomplishment were to arise from teaching, it would be an external demonstration. A demonstration must lead to awakening, and awakening must lead to entry into the Way.

One interpretation states that in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one attains the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha and constantly delights in demonstrating the Buddha’s wisdom, awakening, knowledge, and vision.

Another interpretation states that in the ninth stage, the Bodhisattva is called "Good Wisdom" (*Sādhumatī*) because they profoundly awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. To enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—this is another interpretation.
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes, by means of the Vajra-samādhi, shatter and eliminate the habitual tendencies of delusion and advance into the Buddha-wisdom.
Judging from the substance of this treatise, the stages are thus; yet, when measured against the single awakening of a practitioner, these four meanings are present all at once.
Whether there be two or three: "two" refers to the second vehicle, and "three" refers to the third vehicle; likewise, there would also be no first [vehicle].
Yet the first does not deviate from its nature as the Great; therefore, it is not non-existent. Since the second and third do not exist, the one also departs.
Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise. This is the third section. It cites the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time as witnesses.
The Buddhas of the three periods all first teach the Three Vehicles and subsequently clarify the One Ultimate.
Although the ages differ and the individuals vary, this Way is profoundly identical.
"Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities. This is the fourth section. It clarifies that the Sages do not intentionally establish the three teachings of their own accord;
rather, because sentient beings are defiled and turbid, it is difficult for them to attain awakening through a single [teaching].

Therefore, the three vehicles are expounded out of necessity, as they have no other choice—how could they wish to act thus? During the *kalpa-turbidity*, the beings of former ages possessed pure and ethereal natures, and their karmic burdens were slight. Because...

Now, let us compare these. They are called "turbidities" (*kaṣāya*). "Kalpa" refers to time. When sentient beings are already wicked, they may encounter the calamity of weapons, or suffer through periods of famine, pestilence, and epidemic;

this is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). When various delusions converge, how can the Path arise? The turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) refers generally to the evils of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
As for the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), the five types of false views fundamentally turn their backs on the Truth and oppose Principle; therefore, it is established separately.
This is due to the defilement of the age. When false livelihoods and worldly entanglements intersect, one acts contrary to encountering the Way;

how could this not be called "defilement"? Within the single Buddha-vehicle, the Buddha speaks of three as a distinction. Because the people of this defiled age lack great resolve, and because the principles of the Buddha are profound and remote, they are unable to believe them.
Thus, the Buddha restrains them and brings them closer by establishing the teaching of the Three Vehicles. Although it is said that he teaches three, he is always teaching the One. Now...

It is said: "If one attains Buddhahood within a single human body, does this not constrain [the path] and bring it closer to ordinary people? Since the trace is near to humans, it is outwardly shown to be easy to learn.
If one can learn through what is easy, the ultimate distance [from the goal] will naturally be traversed. It is further said: "The two vehicles are alike in exhausting the fetters (*saṃyojana*)."
If one does not eliminate the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), as one moves closer to others, they become even easier to extinguish.

If one can seek spontaneity (*svabhāva*) through this ease of extinction until reaching total extinction, this is precisely the teaching of the three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Śāriputra, if my disciples claim for themselves to be Arhats—this fifth section distinguishes between the gains and losses of persons—and yet wish to cause the Way to prevail throughout the world, how could they allow such gains and losses to remain undiscerned? They must admonish others to abandon loss and follow gain.
If one claims to be an Arhat yet does not know the Buddha, acting merely to transform Bodhisattvas, then that person is not an Arhat; this is a fault.
To lose this person is to lose the Dharma; to be able to uphold this sutra is called "gaining" it.

Except for the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present—this interval between two sages where there is no holy sovereign—it may be that one does not believe. But if the Buddha were still present, one would certainly believe without doubt.
It secretly influences the people of the time; since the Buddha is currently present, how could one not believe?
The verses follow a sequential order, versifying the first five sections. First, four full verses versify the first section on "the True and the False.
Next, thirty-five verses versify the second section on the "One Great Matter. Next, seventy-five verses versify the third section on "the Testimony of All Buddhas of the World. Next...

The two verses [above] eulogize the preceding fourth section, which explains that the teaching of the three vehicles was given because there was no other alternative. The final five verses eulogize the fifth section concerning those who attain or fail to attain [the goal].
The subtle form of the embryo exists within the delusions of the triple world; it is merely called "subtle" [in contrast to its true nature]. Only the Dharma-body is truly great.

Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful expedients (*upāya*), one assists in manifesting the primary truth (*paramārtha*). Although principle is fundamentally beyond words, it is provisionally expressed through language.
What is called "expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to this. Furthermore, employing the Two Vehicles to assist in the transformation of beings is called "alternative expedient means.

Since the One Vehicle is profound, these [other means] are used as a pretext to reveal it. One interpretation states: that which was taught during the forty-nine years is the [primary] expedient means; what is now being taught in the *Lotus Sūtra* is the alternative expedient means.
If there are sentient beings, even down to those who merely prostrate themselves, this clarifies that these beings have planted various roots of goodness under past Buddhas.
Every single hair’s breadth of virtue and every single act of goodness are accumulated until they form the Way. One knows that all phenomena are eternally without self-nature;

this is the primary meaning of emptiness. It clarifies that the principle is non-dual and ultimate. The lineage of the Buddha arises from conditions; the Buddha is born from the principle of conditions. Since the principle is already non-dual, [the Buddha-nature is likewise so].
How could there possibly be three? Therefore, it is said that there is but a Single Vehicle. This is the abiding nature of phenomena; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.

[This explains] what was previously known regarding the fact that phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature. For this reason, one knows that they are eternally without intrinsic nature. During the three seven-day periods...

The seven days spent contemplating the tree at the beginning were intended to express gratitude. The seven days spent walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*) in the middle were because he attained great enlightenment through such practice;
having attained the Way under the shade of the tree, how could this kindness not be repaid? During the final seven days, he contemplated how to deliver sentient beings;
when the Brahma King invited him to teach the Dharma, he transformed others in response to that inspiration.
Chapter Three: The Parable.

Now, as faculties vary in being sharp or dull, so too does awakening occur sooner or later. Regarding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* preached for the sake of the correct Dharma, those of sharp faculties attain awakening at the highest level;
yet the ignorant have not yet understood it. Therefore, the teaching is conveyed through parables. Since the principle is both profound and subtle, it is difficult to convey in a single [statement].
Therefore, the text employs indirect allusions and imagery to convey its remote intent, borrowing concrete matters to illustrate underlying principles; this is termed "parable" (*dṛṣṭānta*).
From Śāriputra’s exultation down to the beginning of the "Burning House" parable, there are generally three sections that clarify the meaning.
The first clarifies how Śāriputra harbors realization within and manifests understanding without. His former doubts were already profound, and his earnest anxiety was likewise deep; now—
Having first awakened to the One Vehicle, my heart was filled with such overflowing joy that I could not contain it; thus I spoke of it myself, saying:

"To manifest by entrusting oneself to provisional traces is to guide others according to the circumstances of the times. Why is this? Because [otherwise] one would lose the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.

What I have expressed in my own words is intended to clarify this very point. The intent of this clarification is to assist in the fulfillment of what has been heard. Such a Dharma as this—having heard it...
"All sentient beings shall become Buddhas. When he saw the Bodhisattvas receive their predictions, he felt personally aggrieved that he alone was not included among them.

Now, hearing this which accords with what he previously heard, he has attained awakening upon its passing through his ears. In the past, he lamented having lost the Great [Vehicle]; now, having attained awakening, he will surely rejoice.

"I have always dwelt alone in mountain forests and beneath trees; this is not the fault of the World-Honored One. Furthermore, the reason he attained awakening immediately upon hearing it is truly because...
Since long ago, we have constantly harbored this thought: "We have entered the Dharma-nature together with the Tathāgata; how could he restrict us to being necessarily small?

It is only we who have made ourselves small. As for why he manifests this way: the teaching of the Dharma proceeds by gradual stages, necessarily beginning with the small and subsequently proceeding to the great.

Had we waited for him to preach the Great [Vehicle], we would certainly have attained greatness. But because we directly passed over the hearing of the Small [Vehicle] and immediately took it to be the ultimate reality, we remained as we were.

"Small" refers to those who seek realization through worldly gain and profit, constantly reproaching themselves for their shortcomings. Now, hearing that this [Great Vehicle] is one and the same as entering the Dharma-nature without deviation, they immediately awaken.
They realize that it was not that they were not small, but rather that they had been reproaching themselves in vain; now that they have awakened to this, how could their joy ever cease?
"Waiting" is also said to mean "should wait."
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "Among devas, humans, śramaṇas, and [brahmins]—this is the second section, clarifying that since there is no lesser path, one proceeds only toward Buddhahood.
Because Śāriputra had accumulated insights and was profoundly attached to the truth, the Buddha granted him a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Is this proclamation of the prediction truly so? It is merely intended to lead those who long for such a prediction. [Śāriputra] once served twenty trillion Buddhas... up to the Buddha.

This is what is protected and remembered by the Buddha. Because they have attained self-awakening, he joyfully uses irony to bring them to fulfillment. It was not that the followers of the Hīnayāna lacked the aspiration for the Great Vehicle in the past;

rather, their being granted individual predictions now clarifies that within the ultimate principle there is no "small" vehicle. Thus, the distant citation of those who practiced in the past clarifies that it is through their merit that they receive these predictions.
This is not to say that sentient beings are secretly led by the prevailing sentiments of the times. Rather, it is because of his original vow that he teaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

The transformation of the Three Vehicles was originally intended for the defiled world; since that land is pure, it cannot admit of three. Yet, the reason they speak of "three" is to clarify that the three are identical to the one, and that there is no separate three.
Because their fundamental understanding is that the three are identical to the one, they speak of them as such by virtue of their original vows.

How could this be said to be a literal teaching of three transformations? As for bestowing the prediction of firm fulfillment, it is for this reason that he again bestows [the prediction] upon Jianman.
The Reporter [states]: This proves that Śāriputra’s attainment of the prediction was not in vain.
At that time, the fourfold assembly rejoiced with great sincerity and joy. This is the third section: by citing the followers of Svāti, it is shown that they all possess this potential;
therefore, they rejoice. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have no further doubt or regret. As for virtue..."

When the foundation is deep, the concern is profound; when the Way is great, it encompasses universal kingship. Since Śāriputra has completed his awakening, he wishes to cause those with minds to share in this profound understanding.
Therefore, for the sake of the twelve hundred [disciples], he raises their doubts and addresses the Buddha. These śrāvakas, having no prior doubts, [now seek clarification].
Yet there remains the present adherence [to a different view]. It must be opened up and expanded before it can finally be resolved.

This is to hear what has never been heard before: formerly one partook of three, whereas now one partakes of one. Both are the words of the Sage, yet they appear as contradictory as spears and shields;

thus, doubt is bound within that which was heard. The wise attain understanding through parables. The previous statement served to crush their harbored doubts; now it is said that the wise attain understanding through parables.

This draws out their intent. Wisdom has the nature of turning its back on ignorance; since one who is wise hears a parable and awakens to it in their heart, these words are used to challenge them, merely to urge them toward swift awakening.

Regarding the country and city, the following seven sections clarify the underlying principles by means of analogies: first, it clarifies that within the house, calamities arise in competition and manifold misfortunes converge;
second, it clarifies that he alone who has awakened to these afflictions and disasters is the Buddha;

third, having himself attained awakening, the Buddha further gives rise to great compassion to rescue and deliver his children; fourth, intending to bestow the bliss of the three vehicles, he therefore first speaks [of this].
The matters of fear within the house: fifth, granting the bliss of the three vehicles; sixth, granting the ultimate bliss of the true One Vehicle;
seventh, the fact that after initially promising the three carts, one ultimately does not give them because they are false and deceptive.
A "kingdom" (*rāṣṭra*) refers to a walled city; sentient beings within the cities of the three realms are called a kingdom—this is the first section.
A "town" (*nigama*) refers to the ten perfections (*pāramitā*); "perfection" is likened to a town because it is limited and close to people, which is compared to a village (*grāma*).

They share the same name as a city, yet according to their meanings and applications, myriad designations arise. There is a great elder (*mahā-śreṣṭhin*); the Buddha should preside over him. This is [the second section].
That which he reveres is the Elder (Śāriputra). Though his years have declined and he has manifested his final existence, he establishes the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
His wealth is immeasurable; he takes the teaching of the Dharma as the sustenance for the life of wisdom to be his wealth, and its principles being without limit, it is "immeasurable."
There are many fields and houses, as well as various servants. One transforms away their impurities to produce the sprouts of the Way as the fields;

one comes to dwell within them as the house; and one follows the teachings to form conduct as the servants. There is nowhere that is not thus; this constitutes "many. Their household is vast and expansive.
To take the "perhaps" (or) as the foundation and find peace therein is the meaning of "household. Or, being without fixed location, it is vast and expansive.
There is but a single gate; the gateway through which one universally awakens to the Buddha’s teaching. Only this serves as the gateway to the one hundred and two [realms]:
one hundred for the heavens, two hundred for the human realm, and five hundred for the three evil destinies—this is the limit according to the realms (*dhātu*).

The halls and pavilions are dilapidated and old: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the hall, and the two upper realms are the pavilions; their gradual decay constitutes their state of being "dilapidated and old. The walls and partitions...
Ruinous collapse. The multitude may be divided into four groups, which are called "walls. To be overcome by what is unwholesome is called "ruinous collapse.

The foundation of the pillars is rotten; false views dwell within them, serving as the pillars. Being contrary to principle and lacking solidity constitutes "rottenness. The beams and rafters are tilted and precarious;
attachment and craving serve as the beams and rafters, and since their principles are easily subverted, they are "tilted and precarious. All around, they simultaneously burst into flames.
When fire breaks out and burns down a house, it is used as a metaphor for the burning of various sufferings; there is nowhere it does not reach, thus it is "all-pervasive.
It arises from sudden, reckless acts, hence it is "sudden" (*kṣaṇāt*). When circumstances arrive, it "breaks out"; it burns the house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

As for the sons—ten, twenty, or even up to thirty—they have already been transformed by [the Buddha's] teachings, and thus they are called "sons. Because there are distinctions among the three vehicles, they are "threefold," and because they are numerous, they are "many."
Tenth: When the elder saw the great fire rising from all four sides, he was immediately seized with great terror. This is the second section: the Buddha’s awakening to this suffering.

Originally, in his transformative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), there should have been no suffering; yet he manifested it for the sake of causing alarm. [The elder] suffered and his mind became clouded, fearing that his life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*) would thus end in the flames.

Therefore, he was afraid. He then thought: "Although I am able to escape safely through the door that is burning, the Buddha has manifested a form within my house and likewise demonstrated suffering by appearing to enter *nirvāṇa*.
That his life-sustaining power remains intact is due to the power of having transcended existence (*sopadhiśeṣa*);

that he has attained the state beyond existence (*anupadhiśeṣa*) is due to his capability, as well as the capability derived from the prior teachings of the Buddha. Thus, he has escaped through the burning door."

They emerged, yet these sons remained attached to their play and sport; their minds wandered among the five desires for the sake of amusement. They persisted in this for a long time without ceasing, being deeply attached to it.
They were neither aware nor cognizant of it, neither startled nor terrified; they did not consider it a threat to their lives, for they lacked awareness.

Since they lacked awareness, on what basis could they be startled or terrified? As the fire approached and pressed upon their bodies until they had no intention of seeking escape, it wounded and oppressed their life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).
He did not regard this as a calamity. Since the sutra does not describe such a state, why should one seek it out?
At that time, the elder thought to himself: "My own body and hands possess strength. This third section clarifies how the Buddha provides universal salvation.

Having personally realized suffering, he desires that all beings likewise do so; thus he gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to rescue and deliver them. Fundamentally, there is no duality in transformation, yet by deviating from this, they undergo suffering.
Therefore, it is appropriate that he should lead them back by means of the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); thus, he intends to establish the teaching of the One Vehicle.

The "body" (śarīra) refers to the body of traces (*vyañjana-śarīra*). The principle of the body of traces is able to uplift and receive others, acting as a "hand"; it must necessarily possess power. "Clothing and a lap-sack" (*vastra-kośa*):

clothing can wrap and enclose the child; emerging [from concealment] is like supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Being able to traverse uneven terrain and rescue beings is like the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*). The "desk" (*mañca*) represents the fourfold equality; the principle of speech is level and equal.
Furthermore, he reflected that this house has but a single door. This is the fourth section.

Desiring to bestow the joy of the three vehicles, [the Buddha] did not speak of the terrors within the house, for fear of alarming their minds. That which is opened wide by manifold delusions is the "house";

it is narrow and small, its gateways are obscure and deep, and those who wander therein and attain awakening are few; thus the door appears small. Though the Sage, though he may entice them, [they remain] attached to their place of play.
I transformed him, yet he remained ignorant and immature; instead, he became further attached to the playgrounds of the five desires. He may even fall into the fires of the three miserable realms.
Though I wished to transform him once more, how could it have been possible? Therefore, I feigned neglect. He ran to and fro in play, merely watching his father;
traversing the five paths of existence is called "running," while wandering through the six sense-objects is called "playing. He simply watched his father...
Sixth: Failing to reach the inner mind, he regards his father as merely an object of sight.
At that time, when the elder arrives, he is already consumed by a great fire. The fifth section intends to bestow the bliss of the three vehicles.

Previously, he spoke of matters of fear to alarm their hearts; once their hearts were alarmed, they suddenly heard of the excellence of the three vehicles and their minds would surely joyfully accept them.
This was not the ultimate teaching, but what is called a skillful means (*upāya*).

The father knew that each of his sons had their own particular preferences, and that the preferences of sentient beings lie in exchanging suffering for pleasure; thus, he now spoke of the pleasures of the three vehicles.

This is what they prefer; it is a semblance that is not the truth. To substitute suffering for pleasure is to regard the absence of suffering as pleasure, and to regard non-action (*wuwei*) as suffering.
Since the Three Vehicles are eternally free from suffering, how could they be discussed as being on the same level? In their outward traces, they follow the reality of human emotions.
To be able to lead one out of the realm of suffering is the ultimate of skillful means (*upāya*). Since the Three Vehicles do not exist [ultimately], how could there be that bliss?

Yet, to say that it exists is also a skillful means. To say that the bliss of the Three Vehicles lies in the cessation of suffering, yet to neither manifest it nor clarify it because suffering has not been extinguished, is likewise a skillful means.
The Buddha’s transformation resides within humanity; those of the Small Vehicle follow a teacher—these two are likened to oxen and sheep. These are human beings.

Regarding the "intermediate object": the pratyekabuddha, being neither able to transform others nor having followed a teacher, is likened to a deer. Wandering through the three realms is analogous to taking steps;
the suffering of the long journey can be avoided through the principle of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and the joy of replacing one's feet with a vehicle is used as a metaphor for the chariot.
One obtains this by exiting the burning house through the gate of the teaching; therefore, it is said to be "outside the gate. At that time...
The sons rush out of the burning house because they believe it contains what they desire; having received [the teaching], they attain liberation and perform various practices in order to escape.
"Following" means leading toward the escape; one must certainly strive to attain it first, which is why they compete for the front.
If one merely claims it is empty without understanding it, one will instead be burned by the fire—how could there ever be a time of escape?
At that time, the elder saw that his sons had safely emerged. This is the sixth section. Previously, he had expediently enticed them by offering the joy of the three vehicles;
now, he bestows the supreme, singular joy of the great vehicle, so that they are free from all suffering and have emerged in safety.

The "four-way intersection" refers to the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), wherein there is no principle that is not penetrated; it is the four-way intersection in which [the Buddha] dwells in steadfast stability.

To be "seated" means to be free from the further obscuration of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). To be "exposed" (*nagna*) means that each [son] says to his father: "Regarding what you previously promised, we have understood it as such.

Although they truly know there are not three, while they have not yet stepped outside the gate, in principle this is still "not knowing. Once they have gone out, they first realize there are not three;
yet in principle, this is also not yet "knowing one. Therefore, there is the sense of seeking what was promised. However, the Buddha did not grant permission beforehand.
First: Because one does not dare to seek one, three are offered in response before seeking it. If, in principle, there were not three, it would naturally accord with one.

The meaning of "seeking" is thus; this is merely a provisional expression established for the sake of the profound manifestation of the mechanism of "knocking on one. As for the "chariot": [it is as follows].

This refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) of the two vehicles. How could there not be carts within the three realms? It is simply that they are not given such names;
rather, [the Buddha] secretly intends to lead practitioners [to the truth], and thus designates the ultimate state as the "cart.

As for the Mahāyāna, because the Buddha’s true abode is so subtle, profound, and transcendent, it is difficult to approach those of coarse capacity. Therefore, by means of the sixteen-foot trace-body, he is able to draw near to people; thus, he points to the sixteen-foot [form].

Sixth, those of shallow wisdom are like the carts. Seventh, the Bodhisattvas dwelling [in the stages] have subdued the fetters of the triple world; in meaning, they are outside the house, yet they are the ones who seek [the carts].
To each of the sons, he gives one great cart equally. Because of their seeking, it is taught that the three are one principle.

Since the principle is inherently not three, he now gives them one. This "one" is not given as something previously unknown; it was not given for the first time. Originally, there was already the realization of non-existence [of duality].
How could this be a mere resort to expedient terminology? It is merely entrusted [to others] so that those who do not yet understand may be awakened.

The reason for entrusting it to them is truly because people’s worldly sentiments place their trust in me and are unwilling to undergo transformation. Since those who hear of its emergence do not yet comprehend it, they must be told before they can know; how much more so for oneself?

Thus, one has no choice but to accept it, thereby achieving awakening. As for the chariot adorned with various jewels, it symbolizes that within the wondrous principle of the Mahāyāna, there is no excellence that is not fully provided.
It is "high and broad": its principle transcends the realm of numerical calculation, which constitutes its height; it encompasses all things without limit.
The extensive array of various jewels represents the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*. The railings of various jewels are a metaphor for the *dhāraṇīs*.
The bells suspended on all four sides represent the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The ornamental canopy represents compassion. The miscellaneous jewels [represent]...

The seven treasures of wealth are like precious cords; how much more so the great vows, which string together the exquisite garlands of flowers that are the fruits of various virtues—the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment.

These are further spread out as the cushions of the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). The crimson pillow is a metaphor for all meritorious qualities, serving as a support upon which one rests.

The white ox arrives as swiftly as the wind; possessing the six supernormal powers and being free from defilement, it serves as the white ox. Being utterly pure within and without, its skin and color are full and clean;
its principles are subtle and its causes perfected, its physical form is beautiful and excellent; being invincible in all respects, it possesses great strength.
Moving forward upon the Middle Way, his gait is level and upright. Without cessation or obstruction, he is as swift as the wind, spreading the Great Transformation.
Entering the five realms of existence, he travels like one riding in a carriage. His many attendants are those who clarify the teachings and serve as the masters of practitioners;
they wait upon him like a forest. Why is this so? It is because he treats all with equal intent.
"Śāriputra, what do you think? Could there be any falsehood in this? (Section Seven). Previously, he promised to give three carts, yet now he gives only one;
since this deviates from his prior word, it appears as if it were false. Therefore, he questions Śāriputra in return to clarify that it is not false.
He clarifies why it is not false by stating that he merely ensured the sons preserved their entire bodies and lives. If [the original] was truly...
I intended to give [a gift] to those of the three vehicles, yet now I do not give it; nevertheless, this is not false. Why? It is simply that I have caused them to preserve their life of wisdom;
