this kindness is exceedingly great and is sufficient to compensate for my transgression. How could there be any falsehood in this? Even if one were not to give even the smallest single chariot, it would still not be false;
how much less so when there was originally no intention to give, such that the current non-giving does not contradict my prior words? How could it be...?
How much more so when it concerns a great vehicle; then what is gained is truly vast.
The Tathāgata is likewise. Following this, there are seven sections which correspond to the preceding parables.

Of these, the first four sections directly present the internal meaning to correspond with the parables above. The latter three sections first cite external parables and subsequently correlate them with the internal meaning.
Why is this? Regarding the latter three [turnings]: first, the three vehicles were taught; next, the great vehicle was bestowed; and finally, it was shown that these were not false.

The intent behind the arising of these teachings is likewise for the sake of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). The principle of the One Vehicle is manifested in the latter three; therefore, they are first mentioned and then unified.
The first four sections serve to establish the latter three; therefore, they are directly applied as metaphors for what precedes them.

Since the father of the world is the honored one among all things, he first describes his sublime virtues. From this point until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it corresponds to the first metaphor above:
the layout and topography of the house. Seeing that sentient beings, from birth to old age, undergo great suffering yet do not perceive it as such...
[This concludes] the second analogy above, which corresponds to the Tathāgata’s realization of suffering. Śāriputra, having seen this, the Buddha then thought:
"I am the father of sentient beings; I shall lead them to the ultimate wisdom so that they may sport therein.
This corresponds to the third analogy above, representing the Tathāgata’s mind that desires to rescue all things through great compassion. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata further thought:
If I were to reach the wisdom of the Buddha through spiritual power alone, it would correspond to the fourth analogy above.
Because I wish to bestow the joy of the three vehicles, I first speak of matters of fear. Śāriputra, I am like that elder who possesses strength in his body and hands;
this corresponds to the fifth analogy above. Having bestowed the joy of the three vehicles, the three vehicles are prepared below. Śāriputra.
Just as that elder, seeing his children safely emerge from the burning house, corresponds to the sixth [section],
the Parable of the Great Chariots; Śāriputra, just as that elder used the three vehicles as inducements, corresponds to the seventh [section], the Parable of Non-Deception.
Then he spoke in verse. Below, he reiterates the seven preceding parables in stanzas; the first thirty-three verses restate the first parable of the various calamities within the house.
He does not briefly restate the second section concerning the Buddha’s awakening to the manifold sufferings, because its meaning is easily understood.
It belongs to a single person. In the past, when the conditions for transformation struck the Sage, the Sage responded from his treasury of wisdom.

This "response from the treasury" is what is meant by the "decaying house," which belongs to the Buddha alone. That person recently went out, and suddenly a fire broke out. The reason it is said he "recently went out" is to clarify that the fire broke out after he had departed;
it arose from sentient beings themselves and was not caused by the Buddha. The Sage’s manifestation temporarily vanished, which is why it is called "recent."

[The children] came out. Formerly, their transformation was shallow and they were deluded; they naturally drifted apart from one another. By deviating from the principle, they met with calamity and experienced various sufferings, as if a fire had suddenly broken out.
At that time, the master of the house stood outside the gate. These following three verses praise the third section:
the Buddha’s salvation of sentient beings through great compassion. That the Tathāgata transcends the triple world is represented by his standing outside the gate. He heard someone say:

"You sons, you previously entered this house because of your play. Having formerly received transformation and been born as my children, the principle of transformation resided outside the triple world;
yet you soon departed from that transformation and returned to indulging in the five desires as your play, thereby taking on these bodies."
[He did so] so that they might come into this house. Once the master of the house has arrived, the conditions from former causes are likewise activated.
When the faculty [of the sons] strikes against the Sage, the Sage speaks through the medium of human words; thus his response is communicated, and they will surely hear it.

From the following five verses, he instructs and exhorts the sons, praising the matters of fear within the house mentioned in the fourth section above. At that time, the elder had this thought. From the following seven...
One and a half verses. These verses correspond to the fifth section above, concerning the granting of the three vehicles as a reward.
From this point downward, seventeen verses correspond to the sixth section above, concerning the equal bestowal of the great chariots; they do not correspond to the seventh section on non-falsity.
[The text says] "he constructs various great chariots," yet the principle of the Mahāyāna is free from fabrication. The sons did not previously know this, so he causes them to begin...

Knowing that [the house] was being constructed, he said to Śāriputra: "I am also like this. The four verses from here downward correspond to the first simile regarding the structure and layout of the house.
The verse "The Tathāgata has already left the burning house of the triple world" corresponds to the second simile.
The two verses beginning with "This triple world is all mine" correspond to the third simile. Although he thus instructs and admonishes them...
The four verses from here on down correspond with the preceding fifth analogy. The reason they do not correspond with the fourth is that the teaching of fear itself is the bestowing of bliss;
therefore, they are not combined separately. The single verse, "O Śāriputra, for the sake of sentient beings," corresponds with the sixth analogy.
The seventh [verse], which is non-deceptive, serves to corroborate the meaning of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) of the sixth; therefore, it is not combined separately.
If you are able to believe and accept these words: when one sings in a high register, the audience is bound to be small; when a principle is profound, those who believe it must be few.

The One Vehicle path explained previously is its purport mysterious and its reach remote; it is dark and utterly beyond trace. For those of limited understanding, it is truly difficult to place their trust in it.
From here on, it is clarified that one must not recklessly preach this to others. With solemn words and earnest exhortation, may those who face the right direction find peace.
One who attains self-restraint will surely realize this through faith. The Dharma Seal (dharmamudrā) is the wondrous principle of the One Vehicle;

its principle is without obstruction, just as the seal of a sovereign has nothing it cannot penetrate. Since the karmic retribution for this person’s offenses was about to flow down to future generations, he proclaimed it throughout the world via this expedient path;
thus, he established the track of gain and loss to admonish humanity. As for the Lotus Sutra, it is without [superfluous] meaning...
Nothing is excluded; there is no good that is not provided for. If one follows [this path], there is no blessing that will not gather;
if one opposes it, there is no evil that will not come to pass. Therefore, the retributions of sin and merit are set forth extensively to manifest this meaning.

Chapter Four: The Parable of the Belief and Understanding (*Adhimukti-parivarta*). Although the four great śrāvakas attained awakening through parables, because their awakening occurred later, their traces appeared to be still uncertain.

Therefore, they spoke of themselves as "poor sons" to manifest their understanding; since this understanding was necessarily certain, it is called "Belief and Understanding" (*adhimukti*). It is also for this reason that [the Buddha] again clarifies what was previously [taught].
Regarding the path of the three and the one that follows: from the Buddha I have heard this unprecedented Dharma. What was previously called "three distinct [vehicles]" is now heard to be "one.
Thus, Śāriputra was granted the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment. Having heard this voice from the Buddha, it is something I have never heard before.
Therefore, having realized this for himself, what he had attained was beyond his expectations, and his joy was manifold greater than usual.
He rose from his seat and personally recited three verses in sequence to express the reason for his gladness.

From his position as the head of the monastic community until the point where he no longer sought further advancement toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he considered that he had already attained realization; such was his state of mind.
My aspirations have been severed; this is the first instance. In the past, having practiced the teaching for a long time, this is the second instance.
Formerly, when I heard the Buddha preach various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, I grew weary and indolent upon hearing them, contemplating only emptiness and signlessness.
I never possessed the mind to purify buddha-fields or to transform sentient beings. Furthermore, this year I am already advanced in years; this is the third instance, as I draw near to my end.
We are at the end of our lives; our years have grown old and decrepit. Because we are so aged, not a single thought of longing or delight for the unsurpassed path has arisen within us.
Yet now, in the presence of the Buddha, we hear that the Śrāvakas are granted the prediction of the unsurpassed path.

Our hearts are filled with profound joy. Previously, for three lifetimes, this was the fault of our own shores; but now, suddenly hearing the prediction for the Śrāvakas, our emotions leap up beyond all bounds. Thus, there is no...
Measuring precious jewels, they arrive of their own accord without being sought; thus, the meaning of "joyful acceptance" (*anumodanā*) is manifested here.

To provide an analogy for those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), who originally lack great aspirations and abide only in the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), he again establishes this analogy. The following three sections [explain this].
This clarifies the meaning of how immeasurable treasures are obtained spontaneously without seeking.
First, it clarifies that the four great śrāvakas had already received the path of Śākyamuni under twenty thousand Buddhas in the past, thereby establishing the relationship between father and son.
Second, it clarifies that their spiritual capacities were profoundly manifest, and Śākyamuni responded to them by preaching the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Third, for their sake...

The preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the ultimate goal of the One Vehicle. By means of this, it manifests the meaning of the Buddha from afar and assists in perfecting what has been heard from near at hand.

It is like a person who is still young: the first section clarifies the relationship between father and son. In the past, he received transformation during the time of the Bodhisattva; the principle of transformation is fundamentally one.
Being born from the Buddha as a single entity, he is the son, and the Buddha is the father. Having just begun to receive this transformation, he is...
They were like children who abandoned their father and fled. Having only recently begun to receive transformation, the fruits have not yet arrived; they remain deeply mired in worldly delusions.

Whether they run toward the right path or are transformed and depart, it is because they abandoned their father and fled, dwelling long in foreign lands. Yet, within the realm of transformation, things proceed naturally.
To be in one’s own country is to create birth and death through transgression. To be in another country is to go forth to transform others.

To be detained by people is to dwell [in the world]. This may last for ten, twenty, or even fifty years; "five" refers to the five destinies, while "ten" refers to dwelling for a long time—hence the use of "or" because it is not fixed.

Once one has grown old and is further beset by poverty and distress, having been away from transformation for a long time, this constitutes "growing large. Thus, one wanders aimlessly through birth and death.
It is because of poverty and distress that one gallops through the four quarters in search of food and clothing, traversing the five destinies without a place where one does not seek them.
This galloping through the four quarters means that when one has abundance, one seeks great joy—such as music—and when one is in want, one seeks small joys.
Gradually wandering about, one encounters one's own native land. To say that the report [of awakening] cannot be received all at once is "gradual" (漸).

This gradual process occurring away from one's original place is "wandering" (遊行). That the power of transformation should lead one back toward realization is "heading toward one's native land" (向本國). Because conditions secretly draw one along, it happens unexpectedly;
this is "encountering" (遇).

His father had previously come seeking his son but, unable to find him, stayed in a certain city. In the second stage, having attained Buddhahood, he preached the teachings of the Three Vehicles for him.

Since the Buddha had long since transformed others through the accumulation of practice, he constantly desired to find his son; yet because the son had fallen into birth and death (*saṃsāra*), their circumstances were at odds and they could not meet.

Now that the conditions from their past have matured, the son should have arrived, yet he remains attached to the pleasures of birth and death, his disposition diverging from the original intent of his father.
One should understand that while the Buddha manifests in human form, his traces do not reach the ultimate reality; thus, he acts as a provisional dwelling.
The principle of the One Vehicle can serve as a city to prevent wrongdoing, wherein the ten directions are transformed into oneness. His household is immensely wealthy with immeasurable treasures;
although he dwells in a human body as a Buddha, in principle there is nothing that is not the Dharma. This is what it means to possess the wealth of the Dharma, which is inexhaustible.
Gold, silver, and lapis lazuli were all overflowing. The seven treasures of the noble ones could not be looked upon by others;
as storehouses, they surpassed all description. They overflowed with numerous servants, ministers, officials, and subjects, reaching even to countless cattle and sheep.

The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) serve as pages; the various Māras serve as servants. They will inevitably submit and be transformed—this is the meaning of "pages and servants. The Bodhisattvas serve as ministers and assistants, aiding in the proclamation of the true transformation.
The Śrāvakas serve as officials, guarding against and examining what is erroneous and deviant. The sentient beings of the three realms are the subjects, over whom the Buddha is the sovereign king.

As for the elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, these represent the merits of the Three Vehicles, the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and all other virtues. The chariot represents the principle (*li*).
The movement of fortune is without fixed direction. When income and expenditure, as well as profit and interest, extend throughout other lands, this outward transformation is termed "outflow.

This outflow transforms the conduct of others, which constitutes "interest. When this benefit enters those who have been transformed, circulating through the five realms of existence, it is termed "pervading other lands.

Furthermore, the merchants and brokers who appraise goods are likewise exceedingly numerous. The Bodhisattva receives the Dharma to transform the ten directions; thus, he acts as the merchant and seller.

At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages until he reached the city where his father resided. It was the pull of past conditions that led him toward the city where his father lived;
this was the natural course of events.
For over fifty years, the father had constantly thought of his son. His thoughts of compassion had been contrary to reason, yet the son [was now] receiving [the fruits of those deeds].

After being transformed, they wander through the five paths for fifty years; yet they have never spoken of such matters to others—that is, they have never told others that those of the Two Vehicles can attain Buddhahood.
The Great Compassion of the Buddha fundamentally intends to uproot suffering, yet those beings delight in birth and death;

thus, a true transformation would be contrary to their nature. It is necessary to employ the provisional Three Vehicles, which accord with their subtle inclinations, and only then can [the goal] be realized.

This is the first point. However, I reflect upon this myself and harbor regret in my heart; I only regret that my original transformation was not profound enough, which caused [beings] to return and once again wander in saṃsāra.

All of this is for the sake of compassion, and I have merely employed various skillful means in my speech. I consider myself old and decrepit, yet whenever I recall my son, I am reminded that "old and decrepit" refers to my final body (paścima-deha).
That there is "no rest" means that I have not yet declared that those of the two vehicles shall become Buddhas; I fear...
The unsurpassed Dharma-treasure has no one to whom it may be transmitted.

At that time, the impoverished son, wandering about in search of work, happened upon his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate. This was due to the wholesome karma he had performed in the past.

Seeking worldly pleasures, he worked as a hired laborer; yet this was not truly a wholesome way to receive [the fruits of his labor]. Thus, based on past conditions, he secretly made his way to his father’s house.

In the teaching of the Mahāyāna, "father's house" refers to the source from which [the Dharma] emerges, and "gate" refers to the means by which one enters. Although he ought to have entered according to these fundamental conditions, he was pulled back by his worldly attachments and refused to do so;
therefore, he lingered at its side. From afar, he saw his father seated upon a lion throne, with a precious footstool supporting his feet.
In the past, because of certain conditions, he was able to perceive the purport of the Mahāyāna teachings. He was like one who sees his father from afar; in principle, he is the Dharmakāya.
He dwells in fearlessness, seated upon the lion throne, with his feet ever planted in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). A jeweled footstool supports his feet.
Various brahmins surround him with the utmost reverence, just as these gods, though all naturally possessed of pride, nevertheless pay him homage and serve him.

This is indeed how one should be subdued by principle. Adorning his body with necklaces of genuine pearls, such that every form is not contrary to the Dharma, this is the adornment of his body with the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*).
His officials, citizens, and servants stand in attendance at his left and right, holding white whisks (*śveta-vālavyajana*), obeying his instructions with ready hands.
They hold the whisk of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*); in its meaning, they stand in attendance at his side to sweep away the dust of delusion. Thus they are arrayed.
Regarding treasures: their issuing and entering, their taking and giving, and the manifestation of their dharma-characteristics must ensure that the recipient obtains them;

once the recipient has obtained them, the merit returns to oneself, which constitutes "taking and giving. When the impoverished son sees his father’s great power and influence, he immediately conceives fear and regrets having come here.
The father is able to subdue his emotions through his power and influence; the object of fear that his emotions seek to suppress is what constitutes "terror. This includes—

One with the capacity for the Great [Vehicle] strikes upon the Sage to seek the vision of the Father; yet, if their emotions obscure the mind, they are unable to receive the Great and thus come here out of regret.

Such a person leads the multitude toward resolution and acts as the master of the Way. Yet, the multitude being led may grow weary and retreat midway, even desiring to turn back.

If one is confused about the path, it must be that the Buddha-way is distant; one will undergo diligent suffering for a long time, and as the suffering of birth and death is urgent, one may delight in the pleasures of the Lesser Vehicle and take pleasure in them, which results merely in indolence and retreat.
Although such delusions exist, they ultimately do not cause one to lose the fundamental understanding; they serve only to induce a desire to retreat.
To withdraw from the Teacher’s Dharma is to be without concealment regarding the Teacher; the principle is as clear as this.
The Master of the Way employs many skillful means, even manifesting a city. Since there is no concealment, he releases the Master to report [the matter];

the Master then follows the report and comes to know compassion for those who are pitiable. Thus, by means of skillful means, he effects the transformation of the Two Vehicles, saying that they have attained [their goal].

Nirvāṇa: A city is originally intended to ward off wrongdoing; only Nirvāṇa is free from affliction. This is a metaphorical designation used for the sake of expediency, not as an ultimate reality, but merely as a transformation created for the purpose of instruction.
He tells the multitude that they have attained supreme peace and security; such is the transformative intent of the Two Vehicles, expressed through provisional words.
If one is able to reach the place of treasure, one may also act according to one's will. The teaching of the Two Vehicles leads them to attain Buddhahood, yet it does not manifest this explicitly;

At that time, the Guide knew that this multitude had reached the point where they should rest; he had merely said that attaining *nirvāṇa* was the place of rest, whereas in reality, it was a station for those who were to proceed further.

Chapter Eight: The Prediction for the Five Hundred Disciples.

Now, those who are able to propagate the holy teachings and follow in their footsteps do so entirely through skillful means (*upāya*). These gentlemen attained awakening only after hearing [the Dharma] three times;
since their realization was not that of the original pioneers, they received their prediction later. Those who receive their prediction later appear to be dull-witted vessels, yet now—
Since his skillful means (*upāya*) have thus been revealed, it is clear that the Way is not dull or obscure.

Hearing this wisdom is what is called the "Chapter on Skillful Means" (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*), leading to faith and understanding (*adhimukti*). Through the power of his supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), he perceives the supreme matters of great wisdom as if they were happening today;
yet these words cannot fully express them. Thus, the wondrous understanding harbored within himself is known to have originated from the Buddha.
It is accomplished. Since accomplishment depends upon the Buddha, it is said that one cannot proclaim his merits;

yet, in secret, he intends to cause the Buddha to reveal his own traces of practice, clarifying that this is not the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Therefore, he says: "Only the Buddha can know our profound resolve."
For example, there was a person who, along with five hundred arhats, had been slow to attain awakening. He felt both joy and regret as he reproached himself;
his self-reproach was profound, yet his joy was likewise no less deep. Although the Tathāgata’s teachings were delivered without fixed form, their underlying principle has but one destination.

Yet these five hundred people deviated from the words and missed the intent, committing an extreme transgression. Therefore, he drew upon this analogy to express this meaning. [He went] to the house of a close friend.
The "friend" refers to the sixteen princes; the "house" refers to the abode of the Great Teaching.

Although the five hundred men and others had heard [the teachings] in the past, their substance was like plain silk—possessing the potential for being dyed. Upon arriving at the friend’s house, they lay down intoxicated with wine.

The friend’s words of instruction were fundamentally complete and sufficient, yet they were unable to forget those words; instead, their deluded minds became further inflamed, and they remained intoxicated by them.
The five desires and the cycle of birth and death are like being intoxicated and lying down.

At that time, when a friend arrives due to official business and departs with them, although one is said to be deluded and confused, there is nevertheless a subtle awakening from the very beginning. This awakening is indeed subtle, yet from it arises great enlightenment.

Naming the effect after the cause, it is called "priceless. Because it is obscured by delusion, it is as if it were inside one's inner clothing; yet, because it comes through the friend, it is revealed.

To bestow [the teaching] upon a friend is inherently without fault in principle; yet it is also that which binds a friend. There is no difference in this subtle binding. To look [upon such a bond] is nothing short of supreme.
The purport of the Mahāyāna teachings has remained hidden within yourself; you are dim regarding these teachings, which constitutes a lack of awakening. You may still be transformed at the very end.
When the transformative influence has momentarily ceased, it is because official duties must be carried out.
Having arisen, they wander about and consider this sufficient. Their former understanding was triggered by conditions; having turned back from delusion, they arise from their reclining state.

Once arisen, they follow instructions, yet that which they follow is not the fundamental source—this is called "wandering. The *nirvāṇa* of the Two Vehicles is neither a return to the source nor an arrival at another land;
it is a practice performed for the sake of pleasure. Such practice deviates from the Great Way and is fraught with difficulty regarding the Principle. In every respect...
He obtained it. Compared to the Mahāyāna, his joy was slight; compared to the world, he considered it sufficient. Later, while meeting with friends, they encountered him.
Following their instruction, he realized this was what he himself had grasped, yet he had not yet met with his former friend. Now, by explaining three as one, he has finally met him.
It was not by intention that it came to be so, but through a fortuitous encounter. And he spoke these words: "Alas, O Great Man!"... up to [the end].
There is no lack whatsoever. In the past, at the abode of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, I bound the priceless jewel of the Dharma within your heart.

Having attained the intent of the One Vehicle, though my words were merely provisional, by using the cause to reach the fruit, there is no joy you could not obtain; what, then, could you possibly lack?

Yet you have soon forgotten it. At the time you received this transformation, you attained a subtle understanding, but you immediately became attached to the adornments of that transformation, or perhaps your mind was...
[This is] the forgetting.

Five hundred arhats, whose virtue was full within and whose fame flowed without, were therefore granted predictions at the beginning. These learners and...

Regarding the three sections of exposition: first, the "Expedient Means" chapter; second, the "Parable" chapter; and third, the "City of Transformation" chapter.

The "Resolute Belief" chapter is where [Śāriputra] examines his own understanding, and the "Herbs" chapter is where the Buddha recounts his words; these are not separate topical divisions. Regarding the three bestowals of prediction: first, the prediction for Śāriputra;
second, the prediction for the four great śrāvakas; and third, the prediction for the five hundred disciples, both those still in training and those beyond training.
Furthermore, this chapter clearly elucidates the circulation of this sutra. As for the Dharma Master, there is no principle he does not penetrate;

Regarding the reason for addressing [the Buddha] by means of Bhaiṣajyarāja: it is because he is able to burn his own body to manifest the Dharma; therefore, the address is made through him.
A single verse of sympathetic joy (anumodanā) serves as a small illustration for the great; therein lies profound significance. Now, a mind of anger creates a separation from all things.

The Way prizes universal coverage; how could its merit and retribution ever have a limit? Thus, the Tathāgata’s Great Compassion always takes the communication of the Dharma as its concern.
If a person can practice the Dharma, they are indeed a messenger of the Tathāgata. Regarding what the Tathāgata...

He was dispatched to clarify what he understood, which originated from the Buddha’s understanding. That it originates from the Buddha’s understanding means that the Tathāgata, by means of his realization, brings his practice to fulfillment.
Since the Tathāgata fundamentally takes the penetration of the Dharma as his task, that he is able to act in this way is called "performing the work of the Tathāgata."
If there is an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, reviles the Buddha—the most supreme among humans and devas—out of jealousy, this is merely reviling a person;

To insult the Dharma by reviling such a person is to destroy the Dharmakāya. For one who destroys the Dharmakāya, the retribution for their sin is most severe.
This is weighty. To thus encourage the students—is this not magnificent? Thus, one becomes that which is borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata.

What has been said is now being explained. In the preceding chapter, the person was clarified by means of the Dharma; from this point forward, the person is clarified by means of the Dharma.

He covered it with his robe; the principle was profound and fully concealed, yet the robe served as its outward manifestation. The Tathāgata stayed with him overnight, and the lady harbored doubts. Her mind was alert and discerning;

This constitutes "dwelling together. To dwell together means to share a lodging. When one strokes the head of a person who upholds the Lotus Sutra, it signifies that this person is a true child of the Buddha;

What was stated above—that one cannot see or hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra—does not mean that one has not obtained the physical scroll; it merely means that one has not yet grasped the essential principle of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This is what is meant by "merely so. To dig and excavate in search [of water] upon that high plateau is analogous to regarding the One Vehicle as difficult to believe compared to the Three Vehicles;
seeking its understanding within the *Lotus Sūtra* is like seeking water on a high plateau. To uphold, maintain, read, and recite it is the act of digging and excavating.

Just as one sees dry earth and knows that water must be near, though one has not yet reached the profound gateway of the Dharma, this is like seeing dry earth; as one proceeds, one attains ever deeper realization.
It is like seeing turbid mud; once this is known, one realizes that great awakening is not far off, for it indicates that water must be near.
The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). Compassion can cover all extensively, just as a chamber provides shelter through its shade;

thus, it is appropriate to speak of "entering" the chamber. The Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of patience (*kṣānti*). Patience is harmonious and pleasant, just as clothing adorns the body; thus, it is appropriate to speak of [putting on] the robe.
This is indeed so. That which is the Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all dharmas. Emptiness provides space and stability; it is likened to a seat.
A seat is properly called a place for sitting. To bestow such a thing as this—is that not magnificent?
Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa. As for why the stūpa appeared:
it was to authenticate the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, so that its principles would necessarily be clear and manifest. First, it was authenticated by the stūpa;

second, it was authenticated by the sounds that issued forth. Because of these two matters, sentient beings’ faith became even more profound and ultimate. Furthermore, it distantly symbolized the supreme fruit and subtly manifested the eternal abiding [of the Buddha].
At that time, a stupa made of the seven treasures emerged from the earth before the Buddha and remained suspended in mid-air.

Since human sentiments are obscured by ignorance regarding the principles of reality, one cannot help but develop faith through such wonders and marvels. Desiring to provide a manifest proof for this reason, he manifested the precious stupa.
These matters are set forth to clarify the meaning so that it may be clearly perceived.

Since it is said that the Three Vehicles are one and that all sentient beings are none other than Buddhas, they are likewise all in *nirvāṇa*. Between *nirvāṇa* and Buddhahood, what difference is there from beginning to end?
It is only because they are shrouded by the fetters (*saṃyojana*) that they are like a stupa buried underground, or perhaps submerged by the earth, such that its great brilliance cannot manifest.

It is obscured; it must emerge from within, like a stupa rising from the earth. It cannot be obtained externally, for its foundation lies in the principle of emptiness, like a stupa abiding in mid-air.
It then utters words of praise, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! thereby providing a testimony of realization.

Furthermore, as for its being adorned with various jewels, this distantly symbolizes the ultimate fruit, wherein there is no excellence that is not present. Thus, through these matters, its underlying principle is established.
It is evident that although it is difficult to believe, how could it not be so? Furthermore, I have heard that the sounds emerging from within the stūpa were most extraordinary and unprecedented.
When the fourfold assembly saw the stūpa appear, they were at a loss as to why it had occurred; they rose to their feet with solemn countenances, reverently awaiting its meaning.
The matter lay beyond the realm of ordinary emotion, and they did not dare to speak. His name was Mahāpratibhāna (Great Eloquence), and he rode upon the multitude.
They questioned the Buddha and reported it to him, thereby clarifying the underlying intention. He made a great vow;
that he was able to do so by riding upon the past vow of Prabhūtaratna was because he secretly guided the minds of the time, such that all should have resolved to wish to see this Buddha-body.
The reason they must behold his form is to clearly manifest the proof. Only after the emanated Buddhas had gathered back in one place did my own body [then appear].

They appeared. How could this be because they held themselves in high esteem? Rather, it was because they wished to distinguish between the true and the false; thus, it was necessary to assemble them.

The Sahā world immediately transformed into purity. The reason for removing all impurities and evils and relocating the devas and humans—even those who merely offered flowers and incense—was to manifest from afar that suffering must inevitably be extinguished and goodness must surely be cultivated.
Furthermore, he transformed two hundred trillion nayutas of lands; this was because, in order to establish the various Buddhas in their divided bodies, one must first purify these lands in advance.
It is sufficient to accommodate them. Why do they transform gradually? The reason for this is that one wishes to demonstrate that principle cannot be ascended all at once;
it is necessary to investigate the coarse until reaching the subtle, diminishing and further diminishing until there is nothing left to diminish.
This constitutes a single Buddha-land, demonstrating that although the myriad causes differ, they ultimately result in a single fruition. As for dividing his seat, the reason for dividing it is...

Regarding "sharing half a seat": this signifies that the deceased are not necessarily dead, and the living are not necessarily living. The distinction between the living and the dead arises from the various classes of beings;
how could it be that the Sages are otherwise? It also demonstrates the sign that *nirvāṇa* is not far off, so as to cause one’s longing for the Dharma to become urgent.
By means of his supernormal powers, he received the great assembly and placed them all in the void.
The reason he received them was to clarify that the potential for the great awakening of sentient beings is such that they shall all become Buddhas; it was merely to manifest this sign.
Chapter Twelve: On Upholding.

Having already extensively cited analogies regarding those who uphold this sutra, it is now difficult to find those such as the Great Beings, Bhaiṣajyarāja and others, who have vowed themselves to uphold and disseminate this sutra in future evil ages within other lands. It is evil. It is not possible for an Arhat to perform such a transformation; therefore, it is said to have occurred in another land. That he would not consent to it—how could this truly be so?
You merely wish to disparage me beyond measure and use harsh words to press your point.

The Thirteenth Chapter, "On Peaceful Conduct," concludes the exposition on how the three causes constitute the meaning of a single cause. This chapter has already clarified how the various great beings (mahāsattvas) disseminate this sutra;
it is also heard that among the ranks of the śrāvakas, there are those who propagate this Dharma in other lands, and those who wish to transmit this sutra.
Since they do not know the proper method, this chapter is established to teach that method. If one can dwell securely in the four dharmas, then the body will be tranquil and the spirit settled.
Because the spirit is settled and the body is tranquil, external sufferings will not disturb them. When external sufferings do not disturb them, it is called peace and bliss;
thus, one can preach the Dharma without weariness, so that all beings may receive its benefit. The four dharmas are: first, dwelling in practice; second...
This is the practice of associating with the proper objects of reliance. As for "the proper objects of reliance," it means being able to distance oneself from evil and draw near to principle.

Once the mind dwells in principle, then body and speech will be free of transgression; that body and speech are free of transgression is the second dharma. Third is a mind free of jealousy; fourth is a mind of great compassion.
When the three karmas are thus purified and compassionate mindfulness is further expanded, is it not truly magnificent to proclaim the Dharma by means of this?
"In the future evil age, how can one preach this sutra? Previously, it was because the sutra was not yet difficult to uphold;
however, if it were profound and difficult to uphold, those of shallow understanding would naturally recoil. Therefore, he asks for the method to guide practitioners into the evil age.

"If one wishes to preach this sutra throughout the evil age, one should dwell securely in four dharmas. Although it is said that upholding the sutra in the final age involves much evil, if one dwells [in these four], [one may do so].

If these four dharmas exist in the final age, there will be no suffering. Abiding in them ensures peace; therefore, they are called "peaceful abiding. Such is the method of the Dharma of the path of teaching.
First is the peaceful abiding in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice (*caryā-vihāra*) and sphere of proximity (*upaniṣad*).

Having already entered into principle, to put it into practice constitutes the sphere of practice. Although one has not yet entered into principle, to associate with and draw near to it constitutes the sphere of proximity. Furthermore—
These constitute the beginning and the end, forming a single matter. From "abiding on the ground of patience" to "the mind is likewise not startled," regarding the "place of practice":
from beginning to end, patience is the primary principle. These five matters constitute the beginning. Furthermore, "there is no practicing with respect to dharmas."

The preceding section clarified the virtue of the mind that seeks principle; this section now distinguishes the efficacy of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). These four matters constitute the conclusion of the "places of practice" (*caryā-sthāna*).

Regarding the instruction not to associate with kings or princes: association also has its beginning and end. One does not approach places that give rise to disorder, for this constitutes approaching the Principle (*tattva*).
The following matters concern the beginning of the "places of association. *Lokāyata* refers to those who destroy the worldly order.
"Discourse on principles" (*lun yi*) refers to *vitaṇḍā* (sophistry). "Contrary to the Lokāyata" refers to *tarka* (harsh or contentious discourse). Regarding Nara and the others:

this refers to painting their bodies with various colors to create diverse transformations. As for the five kinds of impotent persons (*paṇḍaka*): first is the one impotent from birth (*jātipaṇḍaka*), meaning that although his physical nature is upright and normal, he simply lacks the capacity [for sexual function].
Second is the eunuch (*śaṇḍha*), whose organs are deficient and weak. Third is the one who is impotent for half the month (*pakṣapaṇḍaka*).

The first refers to one who transforms into a woman during the half-month. The fourth is the "impotent due to jealousy," meaning that one was originally incapable oneself, but upon seeing another engage in sexual desire, jealousy arises;
through that jealousy, one then becomes capable. The fifth is the "impotent due to semen," meaning that one can only become capable after another person has first touched one's body.

One contemplates all phenomena as empty, according to their true reality (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*). Although there are more than ten subsequent items listed below, their essence is nothing other than emptiness alone.
This constitutes the initial contemplation, which has not yet entered into the ultimate principle; it serves as the final stage of the preparatory approach.
The verse says: From this point on, the verses may be extensive or concise, or they may not be in verse at all; they should be composed according to the meaning.

Although this does not explicitly mention bodily karma in the prose, it is included in the verse. This chapter may also refer to it as "mental karma."
This ensures that one's physical and verbal actions will certainly be without fault; it does not, however, clarify the mind.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī has reached the state where he harbors no thoughts of jealousy, flattery, or deception. Regarding the third dharma, it means that the mind is free from jealousy.

Although this refers to verbal karma, its purpose is to ensure that the mind is without transgression; it does not clarify the mouth itself. Thus, Mañjuśrī dwells among both householders and renunciants.
The mind of great loving-kindness. As for the fourth dharma, the mind of great compassion: because its scope toward sentient beings is vast, it is explained last.
If one can abide in these four dharmas, then there will be no timidity or weakness; by mounting this expansive teaching, its actual realization will be all-pervading.
It is like a powerful Wheel-Turning Sage King; this analogy refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Previously not given to others, it is now bestowed upon them.

[This] is the meaning. Furthermore, the previous exhortation to protect the Dharma may also be understood here; that it is now said "it is not necessary" has its own specific significance.

Furthermore, those who emerge from the splitting of the earth illustrate that the stage of awakening for sentient beings cannot be obscured; one must necessarily break through the ground of fetters to bring forth the protector of the Dharma.

This extends even to those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Maitreya gave rise to doubts from the depths of his heart; representing the collective concerns of the assembly, he harbored these doubts regarding Śākyamuni.

He wondered how it could be that since his attainment of Buddhahood was but recently, the deeds he had performed were already so vast. Chapter Fifteen: On the Lifespan.
Now, the profound mirror is empty and luminous, transcending the realm of forms. How could there be distinct forms or variations in the duration of life?

Yet, there is nothing that is formless and yet does not possess a lifespan; this arises from the manifold delusions [of sentient beings]. How could it be so for the Sage? It is merely due to delusion...
This refers to the fact that the Buddha’s actual lifespan is one hundred years. Now, to dispel this misconception, he employs the expedient of a long life;

therefore, this chapter is titled "The Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa*). As for "lifespan," it is precisely the supreme mastery of the Buddhas’ supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and is the ultimate fruit (*phala*).
Since the ultimate fruit is thus revealed, how could it be anything other than eternal? Furthermore, ordinary sentiments delight in birth and loathe death; now—
"May you live long. How could this be anything other than earnest?
These are words of ultimate truth. Maitreya harbored doubts and requested their resolution; the Buddha was about to answer him.

This is the height of their thirst for knowledge. They all claim that Śākyamuni of the Śākya clan has now emerged from the royal palace;

Indeed, since my attainment of Buddhahood has been even longer than this. As for the Buddha of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), it appears through responsive manifestation and possesses no fixed, substantial form.
If the form is not substantial, how could there be a lifespan? Thus, the fundamental nature of forms is identical; past and present are one.
The ancient is also the present; the present is also the ancient. There is no time when it does not exist, and no place where it is not present.
If there were times when it did not exist or places where it was not present, that would apply only to material things; it is not so with the Sage.

This is different. To say merely that one "sees the three realms" already implies seeing what lies beyond them. Since the proclamation has its basis, it is hoped that one will seek the meaning expressed through these words.

Therefore, know that although the previous comparison used the number of dust motes, it still did not exhaust even a single hair’s breadth of the Buddha’s lifespan. Now, by representing the Buddha through the form of a bodhisattva, the Buddha’s lifespan appears long.
This analogy, such as that of a skilled physician numbering even a hundred, illustrates how the Buddha truly exists yet speaks of his extinction for the sake of sentient beings.
In the past, they received transformation from him; thus, he gave birth to them as his sons. At twenty, they became followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*);

having already transformed these, he must further transform those, without ceasing. Later, the sons drank the poison of others, and when the medicine took effect, they became dazed and disordered.

To "roll upon the ground" means that one who fails to understand subtle delusions is as if drinking a poisonous drug; being contrary to principle for the sake of others, when the conditions of delusion arrive, it is like the medicine taking effect.

At that time, his father returned home—taking the fundamental transformation and true principle as his home—and because the conditions for transforming him had arrived, he returned once more to the city of Gayā.
This is what is meant by "returning. Among the various sons who have drunk the poison, some have lost their original mind while others have not.
Those who, from the time they began receiving transformation, have constantly practiced the Right Path, are those who have not lost their original mind; to deviate from it is to lose it.

Seeing their father from afar, they all rejoiced greatly at his safe and peaceful return. Because their conditions were shallow and their understanding dim, seeing him from a distance was like gradually approaching the truth;

We, in our folly, mistakenly took poison; now that the conditions for understanding have been awakened, we must truly confess our errors. This is a provisional [teaching].
It is merely a matter of words. I pray that you will grant me relief and healing, and bestow upon me further life.

Having thus entreated for rescue, if one is rescued, the life of wisdom is restored; this too is merely expressed through words. When the father sees his sons suffering in such a manner, he gives them medicine to take.

Other those whose minds were deranged arrived and said it was not delicious; though they knew it was medicine, their faculties being clouded, they took it to be unpalatable and spoke thus:

"It shall be thus at my parinirvāṇa. This excellent and wholesome medicine—the Great Dharma of the Six Perfections—remains here now;

Fundamentally, taking consciousness and sensation as the mind possesses the reality of benefiting all beings. Although the words seem contrary to the ordinary, they are true.

Earth. When affection reaches its innermost core, it is stirred externally. That these jeweled canopies cover this place, and that the Buddhas cause the ten directions to become one—were this not due to the arrival of a response from suspended sincerity, who could achieve such a thing?

Liberation. When the sages initiate the beginning, their principle does not uproot that which has no root. If, within, there is no karmic mechanism for the Way, then the sages would not respond.

Chapter Twenty-Six: The King of Sublime Adornment.
The wondrous Way of the Lotus Sūtra is both profound and far-reaching. Furthermore, those such as Bhaiṣajyarāja have served as its disseminators;

thus, the individuals are exalted and the principles are remote, darkly transcending all common ranks. Those of limited understanding withdraw in retreat, and though they may wish to penetrate it, [they cannot].
I do not dare to scrutinize this with my own mind; therefore, I cite the case of King Wonderful Adornment (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa*).

This King Wonderful Adornment was formerly one of wrong views. Once his wrong views were overturned, he proclaimed the *Lotus Sūtra*. Through this, ordinary people came to recognize it and resolved to master the scripture.

His provisional traces were bold enough to engage them, and those he saved were truly many. Furthermore, this clarifies the meaning of the "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) and distantly reveals the beauty of mutual refinement and exhortation. Thus ends the preface.
This is the narrative concerning past causal conditions.

In the twenty-seventh chapter, "The Chapter on Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s Exhortation," human sentiments are shrouded in obscurity, making it difficult to believe with clarity. One must therefore employ the flexible measure of expedient means, relying upon historical traces and empirical evidence. Such is the nature of these evidences.
Once this is made manifest, one’s faith will surely become profound. The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra originally established a vow:
"Wherever the Lotus Sūtra is read or recited, I shall go there to inspire and encourage them, and point out their errors. This is called the "Chapter on Encouragement and Inspiration" (Kanpappin).
When people rejoice in such spiritual responses and omens, they will certainly apply themselves to the study of the sūtra with even greater diligence and devotion.
Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Lower (End). Composed by Zhu Daosheng.
